Indiana property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • A taxpayer appeals an assessment by filing Form 130 with the assessing official; deadline is June 15 of the assessment year if the Form 11 notice was mailed before May 1, otherwise June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed. (DLGF Fact Sheet - Assessment Appeals; source)
  • After a Form 130 filing, the assessing official schedules a preliminary informal meeting, then reports to the county PTABOA, which must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing. (DLGF Fact Sheet - Assessment Appeals (IC 6-1.1-15-1.2); source)
  • If unsatisfied with the PTABOA decision, or if PTABOA fails to rule within 180 days, the taxpayer may appeal to the Indiana Board of Tax Review with Form 131. (DLGF Fact Sheet - Assessment Appeals; source)
  • The last assessment is presumed correct, but the assessor bears the burden of proof if the assessment rose more than 5% over the prior assessment date (exceptions for new improvements/renovations/zoning/use changes). (DLGF Fact Sheet - Assessment Appeals; source)
  • Assessed value is meant to reflect the price that would induce the owner to sell and a buyer to purchase, reflecting current use. (DLGF Fact Sheet - Assessment Appeals; source)
  • Redemption of property sold at tax sale requires 110% of the minimum bid if redeemed within six months, or 115% if redeemed after six months but within one year of sale. (IC 6-1.1-25-2(b); source)
  • The redemption period is one year after the date of sale, or 120 days after sale to a qualified purchasing agency (IC 36-7-17 / 36-7-17.1). (IC 6-1.1-25-4; source)

Indiana Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Indiana rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Indiana?

It is a deed that passes real estate to a named beneficiary when the owner dies, without a probate transfer of that parcel. Indiana allows it under the Transfer on Death Property Act, IC 32-17-14, and the rules for real estate deeds sit in section 11.

The owner keeps the house for life. The beneficiary has no rights in the property because of the designation until the owner dies, and a sale by the owner ends it.

The statute says the deed works when the owner or the owner's legal representative signs it and it is recorded with the recorder of deeds in the county where the land sits, before the owner dies.

What does a TOD deed need to be valid?

The main requirement is recording during the owner's life. A TOD deed that is not recorded before death is void.

  • No payment is required for the transfer.
  • The deed does not have to be delivered to the beneficiary.
  • The county auditor's endorsement is not needed to record it.
  • The beneficiary can be a revocable or an irrevocable trust.
  • The deed can be worded in substance as a conveyance "TOD to" the beneficiary.

Because delivery is not required, a beneficiary may learn about the deed only after the owner dies. A family that suspects one exists can search the county recorder's records for the parcel.

How does the form of ownership change a TOD deed?

The effect depends on how the owner holds title, and several forms need extra care. Section 11 spells out the outcomes in a list.

Form of ownershipEffect of a TOD deed under IC 32-17-14-11
Tenancy by the entiretyVoid unless the other spouse joins
Joint tenancy with survivorshipSevers the joint tenancy; co-owners become tenants in common
Tenancy in commonThe owner's interest passes to the beneficiary
Life estate measured by the owner's lifeThe conveyance is void

A married couple who hold a house together should not assume one spouse can sign alone. Title questions like these are why a recorded deed is worth reviewing with an attorney.

How do you change or revoke an Indiana TOD deed?

You record a later document in the county before you die. IC 32-17-14-16 says the owner may revoke or change a TOD deed designation by recording either a new deed or an acknowledged affidavit that does so. Unrecorded documents are void.

Several informal steps do not work:

  • Writing on a recorded TOD deed or destroying a copy does not affect the designation.
  • A will or trust cannot revoke or modify a TOD deed.
  • A newer designation replaces an earlier one unless it says otherwise.

Where the owners hold as joint tenants with survivorship, a change needs the agreement of each living owner. For tenants by the entirety, both must agree while both are alive.

What happens if the owner sells the house after signing a TOD deed?

The sale cancels the TOD for that property. Under section 16, transferring the owner's interest during life, whether for payment or not, ends the beneficiary designation for the property. A real estate deed given this way is void unless it is recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies.

So an owner who signed a TOD deed can still sell to a cash buyer. The buyer's title company will search the record, see the TOD deed and confirm the owner's right to convey. The beneficiary has no rights in the home during the owner's lifetime.

This matters for families under pressure. A beneficiary cannot block a sale by the living owner, and an owner who wants to move can sell the house on their own timeline.

Does a TOD deed protect the house from liens and creditors?

No. A beneficiary takes the property subject to the liens and security interests that exist, according to IC 32-17-14-19. A mortgage, a recorded easement or a judgment lien stays on the house after the transfer.

Creditors also keep their rights. IC 32-17-14-29 says the chapter does not limit the rights of an owner's creditors against beneficiaries and other transferees. A beneficiary's liability for creditor claims and statutory allowances is set in IC 32-17-13.

Unpaid property tax is a good example of a lien that follows the house. Our Indiana tax lien guide explains how that lien works. A beneficiary who inherits a house with delinquent tax inherits the tax problem too.

Can a beneficiary sell the house after the owner dies?

Yes, once the beneficiary holds title through the recorded deed, the house is theirs to sell. How long the paperwork takes depends on the county recorder and the title company, and we have not confirmed a statewide step list, so check with both.

Practical points for a beneficiary:

  • Get a certified death certificate.
  • Ask the title company to pull the recorded TOD deed and any later revocation.
  • Check for a mortgage, tax due or liens.
  • Talk to an attorney if a spouse, children or other heirs may have claims. IC 32-17-14-25 deals with the rights of surviving spouses and children.

A house in poor repair can still be sold as is. Cash Home Buyers makes offers on inherited Indiana homes without requiring repairs.

What else does the Transfer on Death Property Act cover?

The act reaches well past deeds. Its section titles show that the same chapter also governs designations on accounts, tangible personal property, and registrations in beneficiary form, so a family may be dealing with several transfers at once.

  • Section 20 requires a beneficiary to survive the owner, and section 22 covers substitution for beneficiaries who do not survive.
  • Section 23 addresses the effect of dissolution or annulment of a marriage.
  • Section 24 addresses fraud, duress, undue influence, mistake and lack of capacity.
  • Section 17 addresses the powers of an attorney in fact, a guardian, a conservator or an agent.
  • Section 32 addresses out-of-state beneficiary designations.

We list these only as headings, since each one has its own conditions. If a family member signed a deed while ill, or a divorce came after the deed was recorded, those sections are the first place for an attorney to look.

When is a TOD deed the wrong tool?

It works best for a single parcel and a clear beneficiary. It fits poorly when the owner has several heirs who may disagree, when the home carries heavy debt, or when the owner wants a trust to manage the property.

  • A beneficiary who dies before the owner raises the survival and substitution rules in sections 20 and 22.
  • Co-owners can undo the intended result by how they hold title.
  • The deed does not remove debts from the property.

An estate planning attorney can compare a TOD deed with a trust or a will for your situation. This page is general information and is not legal advice.

More questions about Indiana Transfer on Death Deed

Does an Indiana TOD deed avoid probate?

For the parcel it covers, yes. The beneficiary takes title through the recorded deed. Other assets in the estate can still need a probate process.

Where do you record an Indiana TOD deed?

With the recorder of deeds in the county where the real estate is located, before the owner's death. A deed recorded after death is void.

Can I cancel a TOD deed by writing a new will?

No. A TOD deed may not be revoked or modified by will or trust. The owner must record a new deed or an acknowledged affidavit before death.

Can the beneficiary stop me from selling my house?

No. Before the owner's death a beneficiary has no rights in the property because of the designation. A sale during life ends the designation for that parcel.

Does the beneficiary have to pay my mortgage?

The beneficiary takes the house subject to existing liens and security interests. The loan stays attached to the property, and lenders keep their rights.

Is the county auditor's signature needed on a TOD deed?

No. IC 32-17-14-11 says the auditor's endorsement is not required to record a TOD deed.

Can a TOD deed name a trust?

Yes. The deed can transfer property to a revocable or an irrevocable trust.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

Selling in Indiana?

What is a property tax lien in Indiana?

In Indiana, the lien for property tax comes from state law, and it attaches to the land itself. Under IC 6-1.1-22-13, each tract of real property is subject to a lien for the taxes levied on it, plus penalties and costs.

The lien attaches on the assessment date of the year the tax is assessed. A sale or transfer of the property does not remove it. If you sell a house with a year of tax unpaid, the lien stays on the parcel until the tax is paid, which is why the title company deals with it at closing.

The same statute says the lien is superior to all other liens. A mortgage, a judgment lien and a contractor claim all rank behind it. It lasts ten years from May 10 of the year the taxes first became due, and that period can stretch if the county starts enforcement inside it.

When does Indiana property tax become delinquent?

Property tax is delinquent when an installment is not paid by its due date. Under IC 6-1.1-22-9, tax assessed for a year is generally due in two equal installments, May 10 and November 10 of the following year. A due date that falls on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day, which is why the 2026 dates were May 11 and November 10.

The Department of Local Government Finance posts the current dates on its property tax due dates page. A payment can count as on time if it is received, postmarked, or sent by electronic transfer by the deadline, according to IC 6-1.1-37-10.

Once an installment is late, penalties start right away.

How much are the penalties on late Indiana property tax?

The first penalty is 5 percent of the delinquent amount or 10 percent, depending on how late you are and whether you were already behind. The 5 percent rate applies when a real property installment is paid in full within 30 days of the due date and the owner has no earlier delinquency on that parcel. Any other case is charged 10 percent.

Marion County states the same rule in plain terms on its due dates page: pay within 30 days with no back taxes and the penalty is 5 percent, and after that it rises to 10 percent.

Later years add more. In each following year, an additional 10 percent applies to unpaid tax on the day after each installment due date. The statute applies these later penalties to the unpaid principal only, so the penalty does not compound on earlier penalties.

SituationPenalty under IC 6-1.1-37-10
Paid within 30 days, no earlier delinquency on the parcel5% of the delinquent amount
Any other late payment10% of the amount due
Still unpaid after each later installment dateAdditional 10% on unpaid principal

What happens after property tax stays unpaid?

The county can eventually put the parcel into a tax sale, which is the main route for turning a tax lien into a transfer of ownership. A taxing unit also has the option to sue the person liable for delinquent tax and recover the tax, penalties and collection costs, including reasonable attorney fees and court costs.

Counties handle the steps in order:

  • The county auditor builds a delinquency list and a notice of sale.
  • The county treasurer and auditor ask the court for a judgment and an order of sale.
  • The property is offered at a public auction, subject to redemption.
  • The owner gets a redemption window before a buyer can ask for a tax deed.

The mechanics of the auction and the redemption window are covered on our Indiana tax sale page. This page stays focused on the lien and on getting it cleared.

Can you set up a payment arrangement on delinquent taxes?

Indiana law allows it. The title of IC 6-1.1-24-1.2 covers removing a property from the delinquency list and an arrangement for payment of delinquent taxes. The details differ by county, so ask your treasurer what it will accept.

Marion County lists a tax sale payment plan and partial payments as separate topics on its Stop a Tax Sale page. The Treasurer's Office can be reached at (317) 327-4444 or mytaxes@indy.gov. A homeowner behind on a plan should call before a sale date is set, not after.

For a house you are trying to sell, a payment plan has a limit. The lien stays with the property until the tax is paid in full, so a buyer's title company will still ask for a payoff at closing.

Does a state tax warrant create a lien on an Indiana house?

Yes, an unpaid state tax can become a lien on real estate in the county where the warrant is recorded. This is a different lien from the property tax lien. After a demand notice goes unanswered for 20 days, the Department of State Revenue can issue a tax warrant, and a 10 percent collection fee is added to the unpaid tax, according to IC 6-8.1-8-2.

The clerk of the circuit court records the warrant as a judgment against the taxpayer, and that judgment creates a state lien on the taxpayer's interest in real and personal property in the county. A filed judgment is valid for 10 years and can be renewed for further 10 year periods.

FeatureProperty tax lienState tax warrant lien
SourceIC 6-1.1-22-13IC 6-8.1-8-2
AttachesOn the assessment date, to that tractWhen the clerk records the warrant as a judgment
LengthTen years from May 10 of the year taxes first became due10 years, renewable
PrioritySuperior to all other liensAttaches in the county where it is recorded

A taxpayer can ask for a release once the debt is satisfied, and the department must release a warrant issued in error. Ask your title company to run a search so any warrant shows up before you list.

What is the vacant and abandoned property rule?

Some delinquent parcels are not offered in a regular tax sale at all, and the owner has no redemption right. Under IC 6-1.1-24-1.5, a county, city or town executive can certify a delinquent property that a court or hearing authority found vacant or abandoned. The auditor then sells it by auction, and the owner has no right to redeem after the sale date.

The minimum bid on those parcels equals the property's share of the county's actual sale costs, not the full tax debt. A vacant house with years of unpaid tax is the situation this rule targets.

  • The tax must be delinquent from the prior year's fall installment or earlier.
  • A court or hearing authority must find the property vacant or abandoned.
  • The auditor publishes the sale notice at least 30 days before the sale.

How does Marion County handle tax liens in Indianapolis?

Marion County states it places a tax lien on homes with unpaid property taxes and sells those liens at an online auction. The 2026 online sale was scheduled for October 13 through 16, with registered bidders putting down a $2,500 deposit for the regular portion, according to the Treasurer's bidder page.

To stop a scheduled sale, an owner pays all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, and a $325 tax sale administration fee. The 2026 deadline was October 8 at 4:30 p.m., and payment is limited to cash, certified check, cashier's check or money order.

Marion County Treasurer: City-County Building, 200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis, IN 46204. Auditor: Suite W-125, phone 317.327.4646.

How do sellers clear a tax lien before closing?

The usual route is to pay the lien from the sale proceeds at closing. The title company orders a payoff from the county treasurer and wires it, so the seller does not need cash up front.

  • Order a current tax bill and a payoff figure that includes penalties.
  • Check for any state tax warrant filed against the owner's name.
  • Confirm whether the parcel is on a delinquency list or has a sale date.
  • If a sale date is near, ask the treasurer for the cutoff time and accepted payment forms.

Cash Home Buyers can buy a house that has these liens and coordinate with the title company so unpaid tax comes out of the proceeds. A seller can request an offer without making repairs first.

More questions about Indiana Tax Liens and Delinquent Property Tax

How long does a property tax lien last in Indiana?

Ten years from May 10 of the year the taxes first became due. If the county starts enforcement inside that period, the deadline can extend as needed to finish it.

Can I sell my house with a tax lien in Indiana?

Yes. The lien follows the property, so the unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing. A title company confirms the payoff amount before the deed is recorded.

Does a tax lien rank ahead of my mortgage?

Yes. IC 6-1.1-22-13 makes the property tax lien superior to all other liens, so it is paid before a mortgage in a forced sale.

What is the penalty for paying Indiana property tax late?

Five percent if you pay within 30 days and have no earlier delinquency on the parcel. Ten percent in any other case, and an extra 10 percent on unpaid principal after each later due date.

Is a state income tax warrant the same as a property tax lien?

No. A tax warrant is issued by the Department of State Revenue and recorded with the circuit court clerk as a judgment. It creates a lien on the taxpayer's real and personal property in that county.

Who do I call in Indianapolis about delinquent property tax?

Call the Marion County Treasurer's Office at (317) 327-4444 for balances and payments. The Auditor's Office at 317.327.4646 handles tax sale questions.

How does an Indiana tax sale work?

An Indiana tax sale is a public auction of a delinquent parcel, and the sale is subject to redemption. The county auditor publishes a notice listing the eligible properties, and the auditor and treasurer then apply to the court for a judgment and an order of sale, as laid out in IC 6-1.1-24-2.

The notice names the owner (or at least one owner), gives the parcel key number and street address, and states the sale place, dates and times. If the sale is online, it must say so and explain how to join. An owner who wants to contest the judgment must file a defense with the court and serve the auditor and treasurer before the earliest application date in the notice, and the court sets a hearing at least seven days before the advertised sale.

Buyers at the sale are not buying the house outright. They are buying the county's lien, and the owner can still pay to get the property back during the redemption period.

What is the minimum bid at an Indiana tax sale?

The minimum bid is the total of the delinquent tax and the costs of running the sale, and no parcel sells for less. The statute lists five pieces that make up that figure.

  • Delinquent taxes and special assessments.
  • Taxes and assessments due in the sale year, whether or not yet delinquent.
  • Penalties on the delinquencies.
  • An auditor fee equal to the greater of $25 or postage and publication costs, plus other actual costs tied to the sale.
  • Unpaid costs from a prior tax sale.

A buyer can bid above the minimum. The extra money is called the overbid, and it matters to the owner because it can become surplus, as explained below.

How long do you have to redeem a house after a tax sale?

An owner usually has one year from the date of sale to redeem, and 120 days if the property was sold to a qualified purchasing agency. That rule is in IC 6-1.1-25-4.

Other situations change the clock:

  • Property on the county's vacant and abandoned list has no right to redeem.
  • If the county acquires a lien that is not sold as a certificate, redemption runs 120 days from the day the lien is acquired.
  • A parcel that was offered but did not sell gets 120 days from the end of the sale.

Marion County repeats the two main periods on its redemption amount page: one year from the sale date for a sold parcel and 120 days for a parcel that was offered but did not sell.

The treasurer and an owner may also agree in writing to extend redemption by one year, as long as the owner pays the full redemption amount before the extended period ends. If the owner breaks that agreement, the treasurer can end it with 30 days' written notice.

How much does it cost to redeem?

The redemption amount is built from several parts, set out in IC 6-1.1-25-2. The base is 110 percent of the minimum bid if you redeem within six months of the sale, or 115 percent if you redeem after six months but within the year.

ComponentRule
Base amount110% of minimum bid within 6 months; 115% after that
OverbidAmount the price exceeded the minimum bid, plus 5% per year (sales after June 30, 2014)
Taxes the buyer paid after the saleReimbursed with 5% per year interest (sales after June 30, 2014)
Certified costsAttorney fees, notice costs and title search costs, certified to the auditor
New delinquenciesTaxes, penalties and fees that became delinquent after the sale

Because the base percentage jumps after six months, redeeming early is cheaper.

What does a tax deed do to the owner's title?

If nobody redeems, the buyer can petition for a tax deed, and that deed ends the owner's interest. Under IC 6-1.1-25-4, the deed conveys a fee simple absolute, free of most liens, with exceptions such as recorded easements and governmental police powers.

The deed has a deadline too. The auditor cannot issue or record it unless, within 150 days after the court hearing that grants the buyer's petition, the court order and sales disclosure form are filed, recording fees are paid, and all outstanding property taxes are paid.

An owner who sits on a house after a sale has a short and costly path left. The practical choice is to redeem or sell before the deed issues.

Do you get money back if the house sells above the minimum bid?

Possibly. If a parcel sells for more than the minimum bid and is not redeemed, the former owner of record may have a right to the surplus, as noted in the sale notice requirements and in IC 6-1.1-24-7.

The buyer's payment goes first to the taxes, assessments, penalties and costs, then to other delinquent taxes, and any remainder goes into a tax sale surplus fund.

  • The owner of record may file a verified claim for the surplus.
  • If the auditor and treasurer approve, the auditor issues a warrant for the amount due.
  • Surplus not claimed within three years after receipt goes to the county general fund.

Claims through a contract holder, executor, attorney in fact or guardian are routed through the court, and a court may direct payment only within three years after the sale. Indiana also limits agreements for recovering surplus money, and the attorney general enforces those limits.

How does Marion County run its tax sale?

Marion County runs an online tax lien sale each year, with the 2026 sale scheduled for October 13 through 16 from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Its bidder page says the non-profit portion runs first, then the regular portion, and that parcels are auctioned in numeric order without a break between townships.

Bidders for the regular portion post a $2,500 deposit, and registration closed October 7 at 3 p.m. New bidders without evidence of credit from a bank were approved for $100,000 as individuals or $250,000 as companies.

Marion is a consolidated city county, so the surplus rule differs from other counties. The treasurer may pay taxes that come due during the redemption period out of the surplus held in the owner's name.

Owners can check whether a parcel sold with the sold parcel finder. Tax sale questions go to the Auditor at MCATaxSale@indy.gov.

How can you stop a tax sale in Marion County?

You stop it by paying everything owed before the cutoff. For 2026, that meant all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, and a $325 administration fee by October 8 at 4:30 p.m., per the Treasurer's Stop a Tax Sale page.

On the day of the public auction, the Treasurer collects payment after 8 a.m. in room 1001 of the City-County Building. Personal and business checks are refused.

Selling the house before the auction is another way out. A buyer's closing pays the tax from the proceeds, and the parcel never reaches the sale. A seller who has already received notice should call (317) 327-4444 to confirm what is owed.

What should an Indiana seller weigh before the sale date?

The decision comes down to timing, money and the condition of the house.

  • Check the redemption figure first, because it rises after six months.
  • Ask whether the parcel is on the vacant and abandoned list, where no redemption exists.
  • Find out whether the home has equity above the tax debt. If it does, selling protects that equity.
  • Keep copies of every notice you receive.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is, including ones facing a tax sale. We can walk through the numbers with you and the title company.

More questions about Indiana Tax Sales

Can I still redeem my Indiana house after the tax sale?

Yes, in most cases. You generally have one year from the date of sale, or 120 days if the property was sold to a qualified purchasing agency. Parcels on the vacant and abandoned list have no redemption right.

What is the redemption percentage in Indiana?

It is 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months of the sale and 115 percent after six months but within the year. Other costs and interest are added on top.

Who buys at an Indiana tax sale?

Registered bidders. In Marion County for 2026, regular bidders posted a $2,500 deposit and registered by October 7.

Can I get the surplus if my house sold above the minimum bid?

Possibly. If the property is not redeemed, the owner of record may file a verified claim. Unclaimed surplus goes to the county general fund after three years.

How do I stop a Marion County tax sale?

Pay the full balance, including penalties, fees and the $325 administration fee, by the posted deadline. The Treasurer takes cash, certified checks, cashier's checks or money orders only.

Can I sell my house before it goes to tax sale?

Yes. A sale that closes before the auction lets the title company pay the tax debt from the proceeds. Confirm the payoff amount and the sale date with the county first.

This guide covers Indiana foreclosure sales according to official sources.

What the official sources say

  • Sheriff must advertise the sale once a week for three successive weeks; the first publication must be at least 30 days before the sale. (IC 32-29-7-3(e); source)
  • A sheriff must sell foreclosed property in a manner reasonably likely to bring the highest net proceeds after expenses. (IC 32-29-7-4; IC 32-30-10-9; source)
  • Sale proceeds are applied first to expenses of sale, then principal, interest and costs; any surplus is paid to the clerk to be transferred to the mortgage debtor, heirs or assignees. (IC 32-30-10-14; source)
  • The court may order sale through an auctioneer if economically feasible or all creditors agree; auctioneer engaged within 14 days of the order. (IC 32-30-10-9; source)
  • Indiana mortgage foreclosure is judicial: the mortgagee proceeds in circuit, superior or probate court of the county where the property lies. (IC 32-30-10-3; source)
  • In a foreclosure of a mortgage, process for execution of judgment may not issue for three months after the complaint is filed (12 months for mortgages executed before Jan 1, 1958). (IC 32-29-7-3; source)
  • Owner-occupied residential foreclosures require a presuit notice; the court sends notice of the right to a settlement conference, which the debtor must request within 30 days of service of the complaint. (IC 32-30-10.5-8; source)
  • Judgment of foreclosure requires, among other conditions, that at least 60 days have elapsed since the presuit notice was sent. (IC 32-30-10.5-9; source)
  • If the defendant pays principal and interest due with costs before final judgment, the foreclosure proceeding is dismissed per section 11; payment after judgment stays the proceedings. (IC 32-30-10-11; source)
  • Court gives personal judgment against parties liable on the debt; balance after sale may be levied on other property where an express agreement for payment exists. (IC 32-30-10-5, -7; source)
